ml-wavefront.title: The wavefront set: where × in which direction

questions.q: By the phase-space-localization definition, $(x_0,\xi_0)\notin\mathrm{WF}(u)$ exactly when:
choices: $u(x_0)$ is finite, regardless of frequency content.
There exists $\phi\in C^\infty_c$ with $\phi(x_0)\ne 0$ and an open cone $V\ni\xi_0$ such that $\widehat{\phi u}(\xi)$ decays faster than every polynomial as $\xi\to\infty$ within $V$.
There exists $\phi\in C^\infty_c$ with $\phi(x_0)\ne 0$ such that $\widehat{\phi u}(\xi_0)=0$ at the single point $\xi_0$.
$u$ is real-analytic in a neighborhood of $x_0$, with $\xi_0$ playing no role.
questions.hint: Two of the choices fail because they ignore the frequency direction $\xi_0$ entirely; one fails because it confuses pointwise vanishing with rapid decay on a cone.
questions.explain: The definition cuts off near $x_0$, then asks for rapid decay of the Fourier transform on a CONICAL neighborhood of $\xi_0$ — both a physical-space window and a frequency-space cone. (0) ignores frequency content entirely. (2) demands vanishing at a single point, which is far weaker than rapid decay on a cone. (3) is the analytic-wavefront variant, which is strictly finer.

choices: $\emptyset$ — the Dirac delta is technically a distribution, not a function with singularities.
$\{(0,0)\}$ — singular at the origin, no direction information.
$\{(0,\xi):\xi\ne 0\}$ — singular at the origin, in every nonzero direction.
$\{(x,\xi):x\ne 0\}$ — supported only away from the origin.
questions.hint: Compute $\widehat{\phi\delta_0}(\xi)$ for any cutoff $\phi$ near $0$ — what is its value, and how does it decay (or not) as $|\xi|\to\infty$?
questions.explain: $\widehat{\phi\delta_0}(\xi)=\phi(0)$, a nonzero constant — no decay in any direction. So no $\xi_0\ne 0$ is a regular direction at $x=0$. The base projection is $\{0\}=\mathrm{singsupp}(\delta_0)$, and the fibre is the entire punctured cotangent space — the canonical 'point singularity has every direction' picture.

questions.q: Match each distribution on the left to its wavefront set on the right.
right: $\emptyset$ — every $(x,\xi)$ is a direction of regularity.
Conormal bundle of the unit sphere — singular along the sphere, conormal direction radial.
$\{(x,\xi):x_1=0,\;\xi=t\,e_1,\;t\ne 0\}$ — singular only on the hyperplane, conormal direction $e_1$.
questions.hint: Two of these have hypersurface singular support (codim 1); one has a single-point singular support; one is smooth. Match each by what its singular support is, then check the direction.
questions.explain: (0)→1: $\delta_0$ — point singularity, isotropic. (1)→3: hyperplane jump — singular only on the hyperplane, with conormal direction $\xi=t\,e_1$. (2)→0: smooth functions have empty WF. (3)→2: a hypersurface measure is singular on the surface, with conormal pointing radially. The pattern: $\mathrm{WF}$ of an indicator/measure on a smooth submanifold $S$ is the conormal bundle $N^*S\setminus 0$.

ml-pseudo-diff-ops.title: Pseudodifferential operators and the symbol calculus

questions.q: A symbol $p\in S^m$ on $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies which estimate for every multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$?
choices: $|p(x,\xi)|\le C_m\,(1+|\xi|)^m$ — only the function itself is bounded.
$|\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_\xi p(x,\xi)|\le C_{\alpha\beta}\,(1+|\xi|)^{m-|\beta|}$ — each $\xi$-derivative drops the order by one; $x$-derivatives do not.
$|\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_\xi p(x,\xi)|\le C_{\alpha\beta}\,(1+|\xi|)^{m-|\alpha|}$ — each $x$-derivative drops the order by one.
$|\partial^\alpha_x\partial^\beta_\xi p(x,\xi)|\le C_{\alpha\beta}\,(1+|\xi|)^{m-|\alpha|-|\beta|}$ — $x$-derivatives and $\xi$-derivatives both drop the order.
questions.hint: Differential operators $\sum a_\alpha(x)D^\alpha$ should fall in $S^m$ when $|\alpha|\le m$ — check which of the four estimates a polynomial-in-$\xi$ symbol actually satisfies for that $m$.
questions.explain: The defining estimate is asymmetric: $\xi$-derivatives are 'cheap' (each drops order by 1) and $x$-derivatives are 'free' (no order drop). This matches polynomials in $\xi$: $\partial_\xi(\xi^\alpha)$ has lower degree, $\partial_x(a(x)\xi^\alpha)$ has the same. The asymmetric estimate is what makes ΨDO composition work modulo lower-order error.

questions.q: Select all true statements about the symbol calculus on $\Psi^m$.
choices: If $P\in\Psi^{m_1}$ and $Q\in\Psi^{m_2}$, then $PQ\in\Psi^{m_1+m_2}$ with principal symbol $\sigma_{m_1+m_2}(PQ)=\sigma_{m_1}(P)\,\sigma_{m_2}(Q)$.
Every $P\in\Psi^m$ is bounded $H^s\to H^{s-m}$ for every $s\in\mathbb{R}$.
Differential operators $\sum_{|\alpha|\le m} a_\alpha(x)D^\alpha$ are pseudodifferential operators of order $m$ with polynomial-in-$\xi$ symbol.
Composition of two ΨDOs is again a ΨDO with full symbol equal to the pointwise product $p(x,\xi)q(x,\xi)$ of the two full symbols.
questions.hint: The principal-symbol composition formula and the *full*-symbol composition formula are not the same. Which choice would only be correct if you stopped at the leading term?
questions.explain: (0,1,2) are core. (3) is wrong: the FULL composition symbol is the asymptotic series $p\#q\sim p\,q + (\partial_\xi p)(\partial_x q)/i + \cdots$; the pointwise product is correct only at the PRINCIPAL-symbol level (top order). The lower-order terms are exactly the structure that makes the calculus interesting — they generate non-trivial commutators $[P,Q]$ at order $m_1+m_2-1$.

questions.q: Match each symbol-calculus notion on the left to its precise structural role on the right.
right: Has principal symbol $\overline{\sigma_m(P)}$ — complex conjugation on the leading term.
Maps $H^s\to C^\infty$ for every $s$; its Schwartz kernel is $C^\infty$.
Function on $T^*\mathbb{R}^n\setminus 0$ defined modulo lower-order terms — coordinate-invariant, the leading datum of $P\in\Psi^m$.
questions.hint: Two of these are objects (operator / function-class), two are derived constructions (principal symbol / adjoint). For the derived ones, ask 'what does taking adjoints / leading terms give?'.
questions.explain: (0)→3: principal symbol is the coordinate-invariant top-order data on $T^*\mathbb{R}^n\setminus 0$. (1)→2: smoothing operators have $C^\infty$ kernel and map every $H^s$ into $C^\infty$. (2)→0: the adjoint's principal symbol is the conjugate of the original's. (3)→1: the symbol class is the function space the operator's kernel comes from after Fourier inversion.

ml-microlocal-regularity.title: Microlocal regularity and propagation of singularities

questions.q: Hörmander's propagation-of-singularities theorem: for $P\in\Psi^m$ with real principal symbol $p_m$, the set $\mathrm{WF}(u)\setminus\mathrm{WF}(Pu)$ is invariant under:
choices: Translations of $T^*\mathbb{R}^n$ — same conclusion in every coordinate system.
The Hamiltonian flow of $p_m$ inside the characteristic variety $\{p_m=0\}$.
The geodesic flow of any background Riemannian metric.
Time-reversal alone, with no other dynamics.
questions.hint: The flow has to be intrinsic to $P$ alone — no auxiliary metric, no global structure on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Which of the four candidates uses only data already encoded in the principal symbol?
questions.explain: The principal symbol $p_m\colon T^*\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is a Hamiltonian on the cotangent symplectic manifold; its Hamiltonian vector field $X_{p_m}$ generates a flow inside each level set, in particular the characteristic variety $\{p_m=0\}$. The integral curves there are the null bicharacteristics, and Hörmander says singularities of $u$ that don't come from $\mathrm{WF}(Pu)$ propagate exactly along these curves.

questions.q: For the wave operator $\Box=-\partial_t^2+\Delta_x$ on $\mathbb{R}^{1+n}$, the principal symbol is $p_2(t,x;\tau,\xi)=\tau^2-|\xi|^2$. The characteristic variety is the set $\{p_2=0\}$. For a fixed nonzero spatial frequency $\xi$ with $|\xi|=1$, how many real values of $\tau$ lie on the characteristic variety?
questions.hint: The characteristic variety is the zero set of the principal symbol. Treat $\tau$ as the variable, fix $|\xi|=1$, and ask how many real $\tau$ satisfy the equation.
questions.explain: $\tau^2-1=0$ gives $\tau=\pm 1$, so two real values. These are the forward and backward light cones in the cotangent fibre, and the bicharacteristics splitting at $|\xi|=1$ correspond to the two solution operators $e^{\pm it\sqrt{-\Delta}}$ — one carrying singularities forward in time, the other backward.

questions.q: Find the error in this attempted proof sketch: "Hörmander's theorem says singularities of $Pu=f$ propagate, so the singular support of $u$ is invariant under any classical PDE flow. In particular, since $\mathrm{WF}$ projects to $\mathrm{singsupp}$, the singular support is also invariant under that flow."
steps: State Hörmander's theorem: $\mathrm{WF}(u)\setminus\mathrm{WF}(Pu)$ is invariant under the bicharacteristic flow inside $\mathrm{Char}(P)$.
Note that $\mathrm{singsupp}(u)$ is the projection of $\mathrm{WF}(u)$ from $T^*\mathbb{R}^n\setminus 0$ to the base $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Conclude that the projection of an invariant set is invariant, so $\mathrm{singsupp}(u)$ is invariant under the projected flow.
Conclude further that this projected flow is the standard PDE characteristic flow on the base.
questions.hint: One step takes for granted that any property of an invariant set passes to its projection. Test that step against a small example: pick two cotangent points above the same $x$ and trace where the bicharacteristic flow sends them.
questions.explain: Step 2 is the error. Bicharacteristic flow lives on $T^*M\setminus 0$, NOT on $M$: two distinct $\xi$ at the same $x$ flow to different cotangent points whose base projections diverge. There is no well-defined 'projected flow' on $M$ — the geometry that propagation describes is genuinely cotangent-bundle, not base-manifold. This is the conceptual win of microlocal analysis over the older 'singularities follow characteristics' picture: the curves live in phase space, not configuration space.

questions.q: A parametrix for an elliptic $P\in\Psi^m$ is a ΨDO $Q$ such that:
choices: $QP=PQ=I$ — an exact two-sided inverse on $L^2$.
$QP=I+R_1$ and $PQ=I+R_2$ where $R_1,R_2\in\Psi^{-\infty}$ are smoothing operators; $Q$ has order $-m$.
$Q$ has principal symbol $1/p_m$ but no relation to $P$ at lower order.
$Q$ exists only if $P$ is self-adjoint.
questions.hint: An elliptic ΨDO is rarely literally invertible (e.g. $-\Delta$ has zero modes on a torus). The right condition relaxes 'exact inverse' to 'inverse modulo something harmless'. What is the natural class of harmless errors?
questions.explain: Smoothing remainders are the right error class: $R\in\Psi^{-\infty}$ maps every $H^s$ into $C^\infty$, so $R\,u$ is automatically smoother than anything in sight. A parametrix gives a left and right inverse modulo this. (0) is too strong — global zero modes / boundary conditions break it. (2) misses that $Q$ inherits structure all the way down. (3) elliptic doesn't require self-adjoint.

questions.q: Which of the following follow from the existence of a parametrix for an elliptic $P\in\Psi^m$? Select all that apply.
choices: If $f\in H^s_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $Pu=f$ then $u\in H^{s+m}_{\mathrm{loc}}$.
If $f\in C^\infty$ and $Pu=f$ then $u\in C^\infty$.
$\mathrm{WF}(u)=\mathrm{WF}(Pu)$ on the elliptic set $\{p_m\ne 0\}$.
$P$ is bounded $L^2\to L^2$ regardless of $m$.
questions.hint: Three of the four follow from chasing the parametrix identity through the Sobolev mapping bound. The fourth would only hold for a specific value of $m$.
questions.explain: (0,1,2) follow from $u=Qf-R u$: $Qf$ is in $H^{s+m}$ when $f\in H^s$, and the smoothing remainder is in $C^\infty$. Iterating gives full $C^\infty$ for $C^\infty$ data, and the WF equality on the elliptic set. (3) is wrong: $P\in\Psi^m$ is bounded $H^s\to H^{s-m}$, in particular $L^2\to L^2$ only when $m\le 0$; for $m=2$ (Laplacian) it maps $H^2\to L^2$, not $L^2\to L^2$.

questions.q: Order the steps of building a parametrix for an elliptic $P\in\Psi^m$ on a coordinate patch.
items: Verify $QP=I+R$ with $R\in\Psi^{-\infty}$, completing the parametrix construction.
Take the asymptotic sum $q\sim q_0+q_{-1}+\cdots$ to define the symbol $q\in S^{-m}$ of the parametrix $Q$.
Define $q_0(x,\xi)=\chi(\xi)/p_m(x,\xi)$ where $\chi$ is a smooth cutoff supported away from $\xi=0$, giving the leading symbol of order $-m$.
Check that $P$ is elliptic: $p_m(x,\xi)\ne 0$ for $\xi\ne 0$ on the relevant patch.
Solve the recursive transport equations for $q_{-1}, q_{-2},\ldots$ so that the symbol of $QP$ has its $j$-th lower-order piece cancelled.
questions.hint: One step is purely a hypothesis check; one is purely a leading-order definition; two are recursive lower-order constructions; one is the final verification. Order them by what depends on what — the lower-order corrections need the leading term first.
questions.explain: (3) Check ellipticity. (2) Define the leading symbol $q_0=1/p_m$. (4) Solve the order-by-order corrections so the composition $q\#p$ matches $1$ to all orders. (1) Sum the asymptotic series via Borel summation to get a genuine symbol. (0) Verify the remainder is smoothing. Skipping any step breaks the construction: e.g. defining $q_0$ before checking ellipticity divides by zero on the characteristic variety.

ml-fourier-integral-ops.title: Fourier integral operators and Lagrangian distributions

questions.q: An FIO $A$ with phase $\phi(x,y,\xi)$ and amplitude $a(x,y,\xi)$ has canonical relation $\Lambda\subset T^*X\times T^*Y$ given by:
choices: $\Lambda=\{(x,d_x\phi;\,y,-d_y\phi):(x,y,\xi)\text{ satisfies }d_\xi\phi=0\}$, a Lagrangian half-dimensional submanifold.
$\Lambda=\{(x,\xi;y,\eta):x=y\}$, the diagonal.
$\Lambda=\{(x,\xi;y,\eta):a(x,y,\xi)=0\}$ — zero set of the amplitude.
$\Lambda=T^*X\times T^*Y$ — the entire product, no constraint.
questions.hint: Stationary phase says only the critical points of $\phi$ in the integration variables contribute. What constraint does that critical-point condition place on the cotangent points $(x,\cdot)$ and $(y,\cdot)$ that the FIO relates?
questions.explain: Stationary phase localizes on $d_\xi\phi=0$ (the critical set $C_\phi$); on this set the cotangent points $(x,d_x\phi)$ and $(y,-d_y\phi)$ are paired, and the resulting relation is automatically Lagrangian by the non-degeneracy of $\phi$. (1) is the special case $\phi=(x-y)\cdot\xi$ giving the diagonal — i.e. ΨDOs. (2) the amplitude controls smoothness, not the canonical relation. (3) gives no constraint, defeating the purpose.

questions.q: Select all true statements about FIOs and ΨDOs.
choices: ΨDOs are exactly the FIOs whose canonical relation is the diagonal of $T^*X$, i.e. they preserve the cotangent point $(x,\xi)$.
If the canonical relation $\Lambda$ is the graph of a symplectomorphism $\chi$, the FIO quantizes $\chi$ and acts on WF by $\mathrm{WF}(Au)=\chi(\mathrm{WF}(u))$.
The wave-equation solution operators $e^{\pm it\sqrt{-\Delta}}$ are FIOs whose canonical relations are the time-$t$ Hamiltonian flows of the symbols $\pm|\xi|$.
Every FIO is bounded $L^2\to L^2$, regardless of the order of its amplitude.
questions.hint: Three of these are textbook structural facts about FIOs as wavefront-set movers. The fourth conflates 'is an FIO' with 'is bounded on $L^2$' without checking the order.
questions.explain: (0,1,2) are the textbook story. (3) is wrong: an FIO of order $m$ maps $H^s\to H^{s-m}$ just like a ΨDO; only zero-order FIOs map $L^2\to L^2$, and even those need the canonical relation to be a graph (the local-graph condition of Hörmander). FIOs of positive order are not $L^2$-bounded.

questions.q: Match each FIO ingredient on the left to its precise role on the right.
right: Where the stationary-phase contribution concentrates: parameterizes $\Lambda$ via $(x,y,\xi)\mapsto(x,d_x\phi;y,-d_y\phi)$.
The submanifold of $T^*X\times T^*Y$ that the FIO quantizes; the canonical relation along which $\mathrm{WF}$ propagates.
Smooth function homogeneous of degree 1 in $\xi$; encodes the geometry / symplectic data of the operator.
Smooth function in the symbol class $S^m$; controls the operator's order, not its geometry.
questions.hint: Two of these are functions you write down (a phase and an amplitude); two are derived geometric objects (a critical set and the Lagrangian it defines). For each, ask: which controls geometry, and which controls smoothness/order?
questions.explain: (0)→2: the phase is the geometric input — its differentials define the canonical relation. (1)→3: the amplitude is the analytic input — its order controls the operator's mapping behavior. (2)→1: the Lagrangian is the geometric output — the submanifold of $T^*X\times T^*Y$ that the operator quantizes. (3)→0: the critical set is the bridge — it's where stationary phase concentrates and parameterizes $\Lambda$.

ml-applications.title: Scattering, Radon transforms, and inverse problems

questions.q: For the Radon transform $Rf(L)=\int_L f$ over lines $L\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, microlocal analysis says a singularity of $f$ at $(x_0,\xi_0)\in T^*\mathbb{R}^2\setminus 0$ is detected by:
choices: Every line through $x_0$.
Lines $L$ with $x_0\in L$ and $L\perp\xi_0$ (i.e. lines through $x_0$ perpendicular to the wavefront direction).
Lines $L$ with $x_0\in L$ and $L$ parallel to $\xi_0$.
Lines $L$ disjoint from a small ball around $x_0$, by an averaging argument.
questions.hint: Picture an edge as a discontinuity along a smooth curve. The line integral $Rf(L)$ feels the edge only when the line and the edge interact transversally — what does that say about the relative orientation of $L$ and the edge's conormal?
questions.explain: An edge with conormal $\xi_0$ is captured by Radon transform values $Rf(L)$ exactly when the line $L$ is perpendicular to $\xi_0$ (so it crosses the edge transversally and produces a jump in the projection). Lines parallel to the edge integrate along it and miss the singularity. The full statement: the Radon FIO has canonical relation $\{(L,\eta;x_0,\xi_0):x_0\in L,\,L\perp\xi_0,\,\eta\propto\xi_0\}$. This is the microlocal foundation of CT visible-singularities theorems.

questions.q: In limited-angle CT, projections are taken only along directions in some restricted angular range $[-\alpha,\alpha]$. What does microlocal analysis predict about reconstruction?
choices: Reconstruction is impossible — no edge of $f$ can be recovered.
All edges of $f$ are recoverable equally well, just with smaller signal-to-noise.
Edges of $f$ whose conormal direction lies in the missing-angle cone are 'invisible' to limited-angle data and produce streak/artifact patterns; edges in the measured cone are sharply recovered.
Reconstruction perfectly recovers smooth parts of $f$ but loses the average value.
questions.hint: Combine the canonical-relation answer (lines $\perp\xi_0$ detect the edge at conormal $\xi_0$) with the constraint that line directions are restricted. Which conormals can possibly be detected, and which are necessarily missed?
questions.explain: If only angles in $[-\alpha,\alpha]$ are measured, the only $\xi_0$ that can be recovered are those with a perpendicular line in the measured set — i.e. $\xi_0$ in the perpendicular cone. Edges with $\xi_0$ outside this cone have no detecting line and become invisible: this is the rigorous form of limited-angle missing-cone artifacts (Quinto, Greenleaf-Uhlmann). The visible-singularities theorem of microlocal analysis predicts exactly which edges survive.

questions.q: Order the conceptual steps that take the Helmholtz equation $(\Delta+k^2)u=f$ from PDE to a microlocally well-posed scattering problem.
items: Apply Hörmander's propagation theorem on the chosen sheet to get existence/uniqueness modulo decaying remainders, completing the limiting absorption principle.
Compute the full symbol $p(x,\xi)=-|\xi|^2+k^2$ (principal part $-|\xi|^2$ is elliptic in the §3 sense) and observe its zero set, the semiclassical characteristic sphere $|\xi|=k$.
Note the standard parametrix $1/p$ blows up on $|\xi|=k$, so a different regularization is needed even though the operator is principal-symbol elliptic.
Impose the Sommerfeld radiation condition $r^{(n-1)/2}(\partial_r-ik)u\to 0$, which microlocally selects the outgoing half of the characteristic variety.
Write down $(\Delta+k^2)u=f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the equation modeling time-harmonic scattering.
questions.hint: Two of the steps are diagnostic (compute, observe what fails); two are remedial (impose a condition, then conclude); one is the prerequisite that the rest depend on. Group them, then sequence inside each group.
questions.explain: (4) State the equation. (1) Compute the full symbol — discovers the semiclassical characteristic sphere $|\xi|=k$ (the principal symbol $-|\xi|^2$ alone is elliptic). (2) Diagnose the failure: $1/p$ blows up on $|\xi|=k$, no naive parametrix. (3) Impose the radiation condition — selects outgoing bicharacteristics. (0) Apply Hörmander on the selected sheet to extract well-posedness. The order is forced: you can't apply propagation before selecting the sheet, can't select before knowing what fails, can't diagnose before computing the symbol, can't compute the symbol before writing the equation.
